text: You get an n by n grid of zeros and ones. Build a quad tree for it. Each node has a val and an is-leaf flag. If a square is all one value, it's a leaf. If not, it has four children: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Return the root.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I look at one square at a time. If every cell in it is the same, I make one leaf and stop. If not, I cut it into four equal squares and solve each one the same way. And for an internal node, val can be anything, so I don't have to pick a special value there. Is that right?
Yes to both. Any val is accepted on an internal node.

Good. One thing already stands out. The rule is check first, split only if the check fails. So a node only splits when its square really is mixed, which means I never create four children that all hold the same value. The tree comes out minimal with no clean-up pass. Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is two to the x, with x from zero to six. So n is one, two, four, up to sixty-four.

That's small — at most four thousand ninety-six cells. And n is always a power of two, so halving the side is always exact. Let me run through the example: zero, one; one, zero. The two by two square is mixed, so the root splits. Each one by one piece is a single cell, so each is a leaf: zero, one, one, zero. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to build the full tree all the way down to single cells, then walk back up and merge any parent whose four children are equal leaves. That works, but it's two ideas in one: build, then clean up. This problem reminds me of plain divide and conquer on a square — like a segment tree, but in two dimensions. The state is a square, and the four quadrants are the four sub-problems. I'll go top-down: test the square, and split only if the test fails. That's the rule from the problem, read literally.

Here's the plan. One: describe a square by three numbers — its side length and its top-left row and column — so I never copy a sub-grid. Two: if every cell matches the top-left cell, return a leaf with that value. Three: otherwise make an internal node and recurse on four half-size squares — right adds half to the column, down adds half to the row. One thing worth flagging — the check comes before the split, and that order is the whole reason the tree is minimal: four equal leaf children would mean their parent's square was uniform, so the check would have made a leaf. There's a trade-off here: checking first re-reads cells the parent already read. Bottom-up would read each cell once, but top-down is simpler. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Is-same compares every cell against the square's own top-left cell and returns false at the first mismatch. Build makes a leaf if the square is uniform; otherwise it makes an internal node and recurses four times with length over two. One thing worth flagging — the internal node reuses the top-left cell as its val. The judge ignores val when is-leaf is false, so on the first example my root prints as zero, zero instead of zero, one, and it's still accepted. And the sneakiest bug is checking only the four corners: it passes every one by one and two by two grid, because there the corners are all the cells. You need n equals four to catch it.

Let's dry-run the code on the eight by eight example, counting cell reads. The row that matters is the top-right four by four: two full rows of zeros, then the ninth read is a one, so it splits — and its four uniform two by two children re-read those same eight cells. Total: seventy-eight reads on sixty-four cells, nine nodes, seven leaves and two internal. That matches. A failing check quits early; a passing check must read the whole square. Corner cases: all zeros is one leaf after four thousand ninety-six reads. A checkerboard builds the biggest tree, five thousand four hundred sixty-one nodes, but reads only six thousand eight hundred twenty-six cells. One odd bottom-right cell gives just twenty-five nodes but nine thousand five hundred fifty-six reads.

Let me think about complexity here. This one is easy to get wrong. Time is order of n squared log n. Group the work by level: squares on one level have the same side, don't overlap, and together cover at most the whole grid, so one level reads at most n squared cells. There are log two of n plus one levels. At sixty-four, the ceiling is four thousand ninety-six times seven, twenty-eight thousand six hundred seventy-two reads. Space is order of n squared for the output tree — the checkerboard gives five thousand four hundred sixty-one nodes — and the stack is at most seven frames, since the side halves every level.
I've seen people say it's really about two point three seven five n squared reads at most. Or maybe three n squared. Isn't it just order of n squared?

I wouldn't claim either. Two point three seven five is real, but only for n equals four: across all sixty-five thousand five hundred thirty-six grids, the worst reads thirty-eight cells, and thirty-eight over sixteen is two point three seven five. At n equals eight there's already a grid that reads one hundred seventy-eight cells, about two point seven eight n squared. So a fixed constant is the wrong way to state it; the safe statement is the level bound. Oh, one more thing — to drop the log factor, I'd go bottom-up: build the four children first, and merge only if all four are leaves with the same value. Each cell is read once. At this size both are instant, so I'd still ship top-down for clarity.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You showed the tree is minimal just from the check-before-split order, with a one-line argument instead of a merge pass. You pinned the cost with the level bound and refused to shrink it to a constant — two point three seven five only holds at n equals four, and n equals eight already beats it. And you named the mechanism: a failing check quits early but a passing one must read every cell, which is why the checkerboard is cheap and one odd corner cell is expensive. Good work.
